response.task_summary: Predict whether an ANES respondent voted for the Democratic or Republican presidential candidate using attitudes and partisan orientations that should generalize across survey years and domains.

ranking.rationale: Seven-point partisan identification is a stable, core determinant of presidential vote across years.
Party identification directly captures enduring partisan alignment and strongly predicts vote choice.
Affective evaluation of the Democratic Party is highly predictive and semantically tied to party support.
Affective evaluation of the Republican Party is highly predictive and robust across elections.
Like-dislike placement for Democrats is another direct measure of partisan affect linked to vote.
Like-dislike placement for Republicans closely tracks support for the GOP ticket.
Liberal-conservative self-placement is a broad ideological signal that generalizes well.
Naming the party that best represents one's views is nearly a direct expression of partisan preference.
Which party represents views best is a strong, stable summary of political alignment.
Whether any party represents the respondent's views captures partisan attachment versus alienation.
Guaranteed jobs and income reflects economic ideology that maps consistently onto party choice.
Government services and spending is a classic ideological dimension with durable predictive value.
Abortion attitudes are a major cross-cycle issue cleavage tied to partisan voting.
Beliefs about which party favors stronger government encode issue-party perceptions relevant to vote.
Gun control salience often separates partisan coalitions and can generalize beyond a single year.
Importance of religion is a durable sociopolitical orientation associated with partisan choice.
Party preference on environment captures issue ownership beliefs that inform vote decisions.
Party preference on inflation reflects economic issue ownership and partisan competence beliefs.
Party preference on unemployment is another stable issue-ownership signal tied to vote.
Defense spending preferences capture ideological and partisan differences that often persist.
Perceptions of which party favors military spending cuts encode partisan issue stereotypes.
National mood about whether things are going well can influence incumbent-party support.
Rating government economic policy is substantively relevant, though somewhat more incumbent-specific.
Retrospective economic evaluation is predictive but can vary with election context.
Views on whether the U.S. grew stronger are relevant retrospective judgments, though context dependent.
Most important national problem captures issue salience, useful but more sensitive to year-specific agendas.
Preference for unified versus split party control reflects governance attitudes with moderate relevance.
President thermometer can be predictive but risks candidate- and year-specific leakage.
Vice-president thermometer is similarly predictive yet more tied to specific election cycles.
Interest in elections reflects engagement and can correlate with partisan turnout and vote choice.
Trust in media may proxy political worldview, though it is less direct than ideology or party ID.
Beliefs about government waste reflect anti-government sentiment associated with partisan preference.
Approval of protests captures broader sociopolitical values that can align with party coalitions.
Education is a meaningful demographic correlate of vote, but can act as a shortcut and shift over time.
Race/ethnicity is predictive in U.S. politics but should be downweighted due to shortcut risk.
Age has some stable association with vote but is weaker and partly demographic shortcutting.
Gender can matter electorally but is a coarse demographic proxy rather than a robust causal attitude.
Occupation may correlate with class and vote, though noisily and with weaker cross-domain stability.
Registration status is behaviorally relevant but may reflect institutional differences across domains.
Trying to influence others indicates engagement, but is only indirectly related to candidate choice.
Donating to a party or candidate signals intensity, yet may be sparse and campaign-specific.
Displaying campaign materials reflects activism but can be brittle and election-specific.
Attending rallies is a noisy engagement measure that may not generalize well across years.
Political organization membership indicates engagement but is not a direct preference measure.
Watching TV campaign coverage mostly captures media exposure rather than stable political preference.
Hearing radio campaign coverage is a weak and potentially outdated exposure proxy.
Reading campaign coverage in magazines is sparse and likely brittle across survey years.
Seeing campaign information on the internet is highly time-varying and can encode survey year.
Belief that one's vote matters is more about efficacy than partisan choice.
Belief that voting is the only way to have a say reflects civic norms, not candidate preference.
Whether uninterested people should vote is a weak normative attitude with limited predictive value.
Whether one should vote if their party cannot win is another weak civic-norm indicator.
State can encode domain shifts and local political context rather than portable individual preference.
Election year is primarily a domain identifier and should be heavily penalized for OOD generalization.
